articleTitle: Ring cameras go mobile as Amazon debuts AI-powered security drone and robot
summary: Amazon announced the Ring Drone Cam and Ring Rover Cam, mobile security cameras that use an AI Pilot system combining cameras, on-device sensors and cloud processing to map indoor spaces and navigate patrol routes. The article examines their operating limitations and privacy implications, including cloud video storage, encryption criticism and Ring’s previous privacy and security failures described by the Federal Trade Commission.

deviceA.name: Ring Drone Cam
specs: AI Pilot uses cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors and cloud processing for autonomous route planning and obstacle avoidance.
Maps indoor floor plans after the customer carries the drone through the spaces.
148-degree field of view.
360-degree rotation.
2K video resolution.
Two LED lights activate in low-light conditions.
Limited to 8 minutes of flight time on a new, fully-charged battery under controlled conditions.
Includes a docking station for charging.
Can follow a set route and schedule for Amazon Ring Protect subscribers.
Can automatically fly along set routes in response to notifications from a Ring camera, sensor or alarm.
Can be controlled directly from Alexa Home Map.
Navigation performance may degrade around reflective surfaces such as polished marble or wet tile, blank matte walls without features, or transparent surfaces like frameless glass and mirrors.
Amazon says videos will be protected with Ring’s Throw Away the Key Encryption.
deviceA.availability: Amazon aims for January 27, 2027, contingent on Federal Communications Commission authorization; customers can register for email updates.

deviceB.name: Ring Rover Cam
specs: AI Pilot uses cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors and cloud processing for autonomous route planning and obstacle avoidance.
Maps indoor floor plans through autonomous exploration.
Livestreams and records in up to 4K video resolution.
Can perform a 360-degree scan at a designated location.
Videos triggered by doorbell rings, motion events and Live View events are stored in the cloud for sharing and replaying for up to 180 days.
Can automatically respond to connected Ring-device alerts by following preprogrammed patrol points.
Designed only for a single-floor, indoor environment; cannot climb stairs.
Not compatible with curved edges, sunken areas, flooring transitions greater than 1.375 inches (3.5 centimeters), and black glossy floors.
Automatically adjustable mast allows viewing over counters, shelving and other obstacles.
Claimed coverage of up to 5,000 square feet (465 square meters).
Includes a siren and light tower.
Includes a microphone for two-way audio communication.
Amazon says videos will be protected with Ring’s Throw Away the Key Encryption.
deviceB.availability: Already available for preorder at the time of the article; scheduled to start shipping on December 16, 2026.

coreControversy.corporateClaim: Amazon describes the products as offering “privacy and security without compromise,” citing LED indicators and screen notifications when video and audio recordings are active. Amazon says videos from both devices will use Throw Away the Key Encryption, introduced in September 2026.
coreControversy.criticismOrAlarm: The EFF describes Throw Away the Key Encryption as an improvement over Ring’s former default settings but still well short of end-to-end encryption. It also criticizes Jamie Siminoff’s “surveillance-first-privacy-last” approach and Ring’s reintroduction of features allowing law enforcement to request footage or live-stream access. Ryan Calo previously warned that flying security cameras offer new ways to surveil people indoors and give companies greater access to sensitive or identifying details of homes and businesses.
coreControversy.regulatoryOrHistoricalPrecedent: A 2023 FTC investigation charged Ring with allowing employees and contractors to watch recordings of customers’ private spaces; the FTC also described inadequate safeguards that allowed hackers to access 55,000 US customers’ accounts. The Ring Always Home Cam previously prompted expanded privacy concerns. Ring’s Familiar Faces facial recognition feature, available for fixed doorbell cameras starting in December 2025, is described as already the subject of a class action lawsuit.

hiddenCatchesAndLimits: AI Pilot explicitly uses cloud processing; its described operation is not local-only.
Both devices digitally map the floor plan of the customer’s home or business.
The drone’s described set-route and scheduled patrol capability requires an Amazon Ring Protect subscription.
The Ring Drone Cam still requires Federal Communications Commission authorization before sale; January 27, 2027 is a contingent target.
The drone’s 8 minutes of flight time is specified only for a new, fully-charged battery under controlled conditions.
Drone navigation may degrade around polished marble or wet tile, blank matte walls without features, and transparent surfaces like frameless glass and mirrors.
The Rover operates only indoors on a single floor and cannot climb stairs.
The Rover is incompatible with curved edges, sunken areas, flooring transitions greater than 1.375 inches (3.5 centimeters), and black glossy floors.
The Rover’s stated coverage is up to 5,000 square feet (465 square meters).
Rover videos triggered by doorbell rings, motion events and Live View events are stored in the cloud for up to 180 days.
The EFF says Throw Away the Key Encryption remains well short of end-to-end encryption.
The article does not specify encryption-key retention or deletion policies; up to 180 days refers to Rover cloud video storage, not key retention.
The article provides no physical device dimensions, Rover battery-life figure, or drone coverage-area figure.

The article does not mention facial recognition or similar person-identification technology being implemented in either new device; its facial recognition discussion concerns fixed Ring doorbell cameras.
